page.title: A million ants in your browser
page.description: Two anthills in a browser tab, where every ant and queen is a tinyactors actor running on WebAssembly.

hero.headline: A million actors in this tab.
hero.lede: Every ant and queen is a statechart, running on tinyactors in your browser. An ant at rest takes memory and waits for its next event.

section.heading: Messages set the limit.
section.p: An ant runs when an event reaches it, such as arriving at food. Your GPU draws it walking in between.
The rest slider sets how long ants stay in the hill between outings. Shorter rests send more messages a second, and the pace chart drops below 100% when the hosts fall behind.

playground.description: Two anthills on a field. Workers carry food home to their queen, and workers of the two colonies fight where they meet.

section.heading: An ant is a statechart.
section.p: An egg becomes a larva, then a worker that forages for 6 to 14 trips. Two fights or a tap end it sooner.

section.heading: So is a queen.
section.p: Once a second she lays an egg for every two pieces of food her workers brought home.

section.heading: The world is an I/O processor.
section.p: Each ant asks the world where to go next. The world is an object in your JavaScript that picks the destination and tells the ant when it arrives.

section.heading: Each colony gets a CPU core.
section.p: Each colony is a host in its own Web Worker, so the two colonies run in parallel.
Every 50 simulated milliseconds, a colony tells its arrived ants and sends the other colony a message about the shared field.
An ant that arrives where an enemy arrived under half a second earlier may fight it.
